prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength bring frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: I have moved from B004 to B041. The chair asked whether my reservation about the lattice clock is a reason to oppose it, and after rereading the round-1 exchange I do not think it is. My test is whether nature supplied clues, and here it has. Clocks at the 10^-18 level resolve the gravitational redshift over millimetre height differences, which means general relativity is being tested in the laboratory on a table-top scale. They also give limits on drifts of constants, and they let a many-body quantum system be used as a clock. That is a change in what physics can observe, and it is not only a better instrument. Katori's magic-wavelength idea is a specific, original invention and the realisation by Katori and Ye is reproduced and compared in many independent laboratories. The two-name credit is clean, whereas my own B004 needs a trio that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan make hard to defend. I would still ask for a citation that names the lattice and the magic wavelength and leaves the 2005 and 2012 prizes where they are.
statement.case_against: The honest reservation remains that the strongest fundamental-physics payoffs (varying constants, dark-matter searches, a redefinition of the second) are prospective, and that the constant-variation results so far are null. A committee that wants a new phenomenon in nature, and not a record measurement, can fairly call this a refinement of ground already honoured by the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. Two names also cannot reflect the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups to the accuracy evaluation. I remain unsure that the cosmic or existential reach we sometimes look for is present, and B004 and B029 stay stronger on conceptual or observational novelty, but both have unresolved credit problems.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is reproduced across RIKEN, JILA, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, has a clean pair of names, and that the committee's support comes from members with different specialties.
responses.response: That is the argument that moved me. Independent reproduction is the experimentalist's test, and I should apply it as hard to my own preferred candidate as to others. B041 passes it more cleanly than B004 does, where the credit is contested. I still think the payoff for fundamental physics is mostly ahead, so I would like the citation to be honest about that and rest on the invention and the realisation, not on promised tests. I accept your wording on the magic-wavelength lattice, and I would adopt it nearly as written.

responses.point: Lindroth says the lattice clock has a clear before and after, because it resolves the redshift over millimetres and constrains constants, and that it is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: The millimetre redshift is the point that changed my view of discovery content, since it is a clue from nature obtained in a laboratory and not only a metrology number. I agree that the citation should lead with the lattice clock itself, as you and Johansson ask, and not with a list of applications. Your own caution about bias towards precision atomic physics is fair, but I do not see it here, since a theorist from outside the field has now reached the same conclusion. On the 2016 question for B004, I still hold my round-1 view, but I accept that it is not enough to carry a case with an unresolved trio.

responses.point: Johansson wants a citation that names the concept and the first record-level realisations, so that NIST, PTB and SYRTE are not implicitly excluded, and notes that the new-physics claims are still prospective.
responses.response: I agree and I would go slightly further. The citation should say what has been done (invention of the lattice clock and accuracy at the 10^-18 level) and should not mention dark matter or varying constants, because the committee should only reward what has been demonstrated. Your own phrase on opening new tests of fundamental physics is acceptable to me as a statement of consequence, but I prefer to leave it out of the citation to avoid inviting disputes over priority. I share your concern about the two-name limit and I think the committee should be open that the wider clock community made essential contributions.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, treats B041 as the strongest on the shortlist but admits that novelty relative to the comb and ion-control prizes is the main objection, and keeps IceCube and GRB afterglows as fallbacks.
responses.response: I accept the objection and I think it is answered by the citation, not by dropping the candidate. On IceCube, I still see it as the most interesting challenger as a new window, but the three-sigma source evidence and a collaboration of several hundred people leave no defensible cut at three names, which you also say. So I keep B029 as an alternative but do not propose it as the preferred part.

responses.point: Olsson says the verified invention, not the downstream decision of the metrology bodies on the second, is the discovery criterion, and that the historical record on who did the original experiment is short and localised.
responses.response: I think that is right and it answers a reservation I voiced in round 1. A prize does not have to wait for the redefinition of the second, and I would be wrong to apply a stricter test here than to, say, topological insulators. I agree with you that the record is short and well localised for Katori's first strontium demonstration and for Ye's push to the 10^-18 level. That supports two names without the squeeze I could not avoid with B004.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges a precision-measurement prize acceptable this year given the 2005 and 2012 clock-related prizes, and whether my own earlier doubt about instrumentation versus discovery was too severe.
Whether the citation wording can separate the lattice clock from earlier prizes while leaving room for the NIST, PTB and SYRTE contributions that two names cannot cover.
Whether the 2016 topological prize is judged to overlap B004 enough to defeat it, and whether Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan can be bypassed, which is why I no longer prefer it.
I am relying on my recollection of the priority chronology and of the latest accuracy records and have not verified them against the dossiers.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict applies to the B041 names Katori and Ye, and I have no collaboration or supervisory tie to either. I am a string theorist and so outside the field of atomic clocks, which I note as a limit on my judgement of the priority detail and not as a conflict. My earlier note on B029 stands: Uppsala researchers take part in IceCube-type collaborations, but I have no tie to the credited names and B029 is only an alternative.
